units: two different routes lead to the same high crossing point
one of them climbs a steep face whose ground is covered with stones
on that steep route the walkers move up in tight switchbacks
the other route loops around a soft rolling landform
the gentle route runs one and a half times longer than the steep one
its unchanging grade lets a walker hold an even pace
workers record the height, the width and the ground type every season
on the steep way they set wooden steps pinned down with stakes
on the gentle way they cut channels to carry the water off
a heavily loaded walker will take the less steep way
text: Two footpaths converge on the same high pass, yet their layouts have nothing in common. One attacks the steep face directly, across ground buried under loose stone, so walkers climb in tight switchbacks, planting each boot squarely on tilted slabs. The other swings wide around a soft, rolling shoulder of the range. It measures half again as long as the steep line, but its gradient never varies, which allows a steady pace from bottom to summit. Maintenance crews survey both paths every season, recording the rise, the usable width, and the composition of the surface. On the steep line they install wooden steps anchored by stakes. On the gentler one they cut shallow channels along the edge to drain the runoff. Anyone carrying a heavy pack chooses the easier gradient; whoever races the mist to the ridge chooses the other.

units: the writer looks at the reasons that push people to go far away
he counts three motives shared by most travelers
the first is the change of setting, which sharpens attention
the second is the exchange with those who live on the spot
the writer holds conversation above mere looking
the third motive consists in piling up places visited
this piling up is criticized because it turns a site into a catch
the writer advises going more slowly and staying on the spot
he suggests giving up any trace brought home from the journey
text: It is worth asking what exactly we are after when we travel into distant country. Three motives recur among the majority of travelers. The first is the break with familiar scenery: the eye confronts a horizon whose rules it does not know, and that ignorance sharpens attention. The second is the exchange with the people who actually live there, since a conversation with a herder, a fisherman or a weaver counts for more than contemplating endless views. The third, harder to admit, is accumulation: one hoards landscapes the way others stack up printed tokens. This last motive deserves severe scrutiny, because it converts a limpid valley into a trophy and the traveler into a bookkeeper of his own exploits. An ethics of movement would mean slowing down, remaining in place, and surrendering any proof that the journey ever happened.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman described leads walkers in the mountains
her father raised cattle
she spent her childhood in an isolated cluster of houses
very young, she drove the animals along soaked tracks
she followed a training course where she learned to read maps
that course also covered rescue work on difficult ground
she came back to her valley with a certificate to guide visitors
she can judge a group's exhaustion from the way it walks
she now trains future guides
she says the only thing she misses from her father's work is the smell of fodder
text: Her father raised cattle, and the high-valley guide spent her childhood in a cluster of houses where the road expired at the last meadow. As a small girl she drove the animals along waterlogged tracks and learned to read the sky before the other children did. In her teens she left for a training school, where she studied cartography and the techniques of rescue on broken ground. She returned home holding a certificate and offered her services to walkers passing through. Across roughly ten seasons she led parties up to the ridges and learned to gauge a group's exhaustion from its gait alone. Now she teaches: young guides come to her for slopes, for the choice of resting places, and for the art of announcing that a climb is finished. Of her father's trade she misses only the smell of cut hay.

units: the speaker was let down by a walk along the sea
the leaflet announced a shoreline left in its natural state
the path had in fact been widened to let machines through
a railing runs the whole length of the route
that railing hides the drop and removes the sense of danger
the walker ends up watching the ground instead of the landscape
the gravel surface turns dangerous under a fine rain
the final part of the route becomes narrow and wild again
the speaker finds there the interest he expected from the outing
text: Honestly, that coastal walk thoroughly disappointed me, and it took a while to work out exactly why. The leaflet promised a shoreline preserved in its original state. What you actually walk is a track widened for maintenance machinery, bordered by an unbroken railing. Since that railing conceals the drop, you lose the sense of exposure that makes a clifftop worth anything. So you move quickly, you watch your feet, and nothing remains to fear or to admire. On top of that they spread gravel over the surface, which turns slippery the moment a fine rain begins, forcing you to brake without offering a scrap of satisfaction in return. Only the final stretch redeems the outing. There the path narrows again, a heavy sea hammers the rocks, and you finally get what brought you to this coast.

units: the writer of the message is staying at a mountain inn
the local economy depends on walkers coming through
rainfall brought down a long part of the usual path
bookings were cancelled and the lodging emptied out
a solution was found after three evenings of argument
the women of the place suggested a replacement route on the other flank
a woodworker is building a log bridge over a soaked hollow
the postal employee drew the new route on a public map
the walkers came back the following week
text: I am writing to you from a mountain inn, and I will lay the situation out the way a reporter would. The hamlet lives on the walkers who come through, but heavy rainfall brought down a long stretch of the principal path. The bookings evaporated, the rooms emptied, and the innkeeper talks about a season already lost. A way out emerged over three evenings of argument. The women here proposed opening a replacement route along the shaded flank, longer but perfectly walkable. A carpenter is assembling a bridge of logs above the waterlogged gully. The postman, who knows every shortcut in the district, traced the changed route on a map posted at the entrance to the village. The walkers returned the following week. I leave tomorrow by that very path and I will tell you afterwards what it is worth.

units: the question put sets the seashore against the summits
an old walker answers by asking what one wants from walking
he links flat expanses to the dissolving of the self
he explains that flat country wipes out landmarks
he links the summits to physical hardship
effort at altitude brings the walker back to the feel of his skeleton
he is asked which setting leaves the most lasting mark
he picks the emptiest setting, because it offers little to memorize
he sets that emptiness against a rich valley that scatters into small details
he states that one never finds the place as one left it
text: Should one choose the shoreline or the heights? To that question an old walker responded with another: what do you want from walking? If you want to lose yourself, he said, flat country serves better, because it obliterates landmarks and lets the mind drift beneath a hazy sky. If you want an ordeal, the ridge prevails, since every step exacts payment and the effort restores to the walker an awareness of his own bones. He was asked next which of the two scenes lodges longest in the memory. He chose the barest without hesitating. An open expanse with neither tree nor house is retained precisely because it offers almost nothing to retain, whereas a fertile valley crumbles into countless small details. The last question concerned the return. You never come back, he said, smiling, to the place you left.

units: a rock specialist teaches how to examine a slope before climbing it
a rock that splits into sheets lets water work its way in
that kind of ground turns dangerous after rain
a flank under bushes holds better than a flank with no plants
the roots hold the loose part of the ground in place
a side kept from the sun keeps its water longer
flat surfaces on a slope reveal past slides
a member of the group asks the specialist about gullies that look dry
the answer is that a stony bed fills with water during a downpour
the closing advice is to avoid any steep slope whose way out cannot be seen
text: The rock specialist demonstrated to the group how to read a slope before setting foot on it. He began with the stone itself: wherever it splits into flat sheets, water infiltrates, and the ground turns slippery once rain has fallen. He moved on afterwards to vegetation. A slope under scrub holds together better than a bare bank, because the roots grip the loose upper layer. He added that a flank kept out of the sunlight remains damp long after the rest has dried. Last came the shape of the terrain, and he dwelt on the flat shelves, which betray older landslides. Someone in the group asked whether a gully can be trusted when it appears dry. Not at all, he replied: a stony bed fills up in a single downpour. He finished by advising them to skirt any steep passage whose exit they cannot see.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the high crossings first served practical needs
goods carriers opened the first ways
those ways took up the lines worn in by herds
builders then put up works spanning the watercourses
those works cut several weeks off the journeys
travel stayed limited to traders and letter carriers
scholars later climbed the summits out of pure curiosity
their published accounts created a taste for steep country
the earlier generation found that country ugly
the boring of tunnels did away with the hardship of the crossing
text: Crossing the high passes began as a practical necessity, not a pleasure. The earliest routes were opened by carriers hauling salt and wool, who followed the lines of least effort that grazing herds had already worn into the ground. Then came the bridge builders, capable of throwing an arch above a torrent and cutting half a season off a journey. Travel nonetheless remained the business of merchants and letter carriers. Later, scholars undertook to climb the summits from curiosity alone, loaded with measuring instruments and notebooks, and people took them at first for men who had lost their way. Their accounts, printed and circulated, bred a taste for broken country that the preceding generation had considered hideous. At last transport companies bored through the rock, and the pass ceased to be an ordeal.

units: the clearness of a high lake comes from what the water carries
lowland rivers drag along sediment torn from farmed banks
those fine materials hang in the water and hinder sight
up high the area feeding the lake is short and the rock is hard
so the water tears very little material away
the cold limits the spread of microscopic plants
that scarcity of algae raises the clearness of the water further
a walker sees the stones on the bottom and misjudges the depth
the lack of food keeps animal life scarce and fish growth very slow
work upstream can cloud the water for a whole season
text: The water of a mountain lake looks transparent because of what it carries. Lowland rivers drag along silt torn from cultivated banks, and those fine particles remain suspended in the current and blur whatever you try to see. Higher up, the catchment area feeding the lake is short and the rock is hard, so the water strips almost nothing away. The cold restrains the spread of algae, which sharpens the clarity further still. A walker makes out the pebbles on the bottom and mistakes a genuine depth for an insignificant dip. That clarity comes with a price attached. With so little nourishment in the water, animal life remains scarce and fish put on weight at a crawl. A single work site upstream, stirring the mud of some old deposit, is enough to cloud the whole lake for an entire season.

units: two walkers meant to cross a flat wind-exposed expanse without a stop
they had set out with little gear
a thick veil of vapour came down halfway across
the way was marked by small piles of stones
those markers became invisible
one of the two proposed pushing on by guesswork
the narrator refused because of the holes where one can get hurt
they worked out a way of moving where one waits while the other scouts
the one moving ahead calls out as soon as he spots the next marker
the veil lifted near a grassy hollow, close to the shelter
text: We had it in our heads to cross the windswept plateau in a single push, light packs, map folded into a pocket. Bad calculation. Halfway over, the fog dropped without warning and the trail, marked by modest heaps of stones, vanished. My companion wanted to continue by guesswork. I refused, because a plateau like that is pitted with cavities where you snap a bone in your foot. So we devised a method. One of us stayed motionless beside the last visible marker while the other advanced straight ahead to the limit of visibility, shouting continuously. The instant he spotted the next heap, he called, and his partner joined him. We progressed that way, relay after relay, the whole afternoon. The fog lifted at the lip of a grassy hollow, and the shelter stood there, within earshot.
